sections.title: Woord Vooraf In Memoriam (p.2)
sections.text: FOREWORD In your hands is the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2018. In this report, you can read about the deployments the Navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The Navy once again made a significant impression during the Navy Days in Den Helder. Additionally, this year featured Velas Latinoamérica Curaçao, a unique celebration where several tall ships visited Willemstad. The Navy was also represented there. With many visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the Navy has to offer. The personnel underwent many new training programs and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the Navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword by Commander (kltz) Rob Kramer, Commander of Naval Forces.

At CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command), several projects turned out to be more expensive than anticipated, such as the maintenance of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam and a high number of unexpected breakdowns due to the aging fleet. In 2018, forty million euros were added to the budget because the Caribbean Coast Guard was included in the CZSK budget. This year, CZSK entered into significantly more obligations than in 2018. As part of the effort to achieve more simplicity and effectiveness, a pilot project was initiated on October 1, 2017, to test the independent small purchases (ZKA) process for 'small items'. In addition, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within the CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and constitutional and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different bureaus. This way, every employee at JUZA can function as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel, but does assist them as needed. In criminal or disciplinary cases, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter. Personnel and Organization (P&O) Head: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P. Damen, from July 1, Captain (ktz) E.C.W. Jansen General Just like previous years, 2018 was a turbulent year. CZSK faced a significant shortage of personnel. To limit the outflow, the Technical Service (TD) allowances established in 2016 were applied and utilized more broadly. By limiting personnel transfers, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam is in dry dock at Damen Shiprepair for the second part of the maintenance program.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4)
sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2018_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate of Personnel and Operations adjustments had to be made to the assignments of the operational units. In some cases, this led to the cancellation of assignments. In addition, further guidelines were received to optimally but clustered distribute the available operational personnel across the Major Surface Units (GBW). In 2017, the project Development of the Armed Forces (DOKM) was initiated, for which a project organization had already been established. For CZSK, DOKM involved the expansion of operational (combat) support. In the coming years, these expansions will be implemented and will lead to, among other things, the expansion of mine countermeasure capacity, the establishment of the Fleet Marine Squadron, and a second supply ship. These promising future prospects resulted in the growth of the CZSK organization. This made it more challenging to provide the organization with sufficiently motivated and well-trained personnel. To attract future civilian personnel, the 'Pool of 100' was introduced. Personnel who do not yet have a position but expect to within three years due to the aging within the Directorate of Maritime Maintenance (DMI) had temporary placement within this Pool. This allowed them to participate in the application process from within the organization. Career Guidance Career guidance explored future possibilities together with the employee based on personal wishes and what the organization had to offer in terms of positions. This exploration took place in the form of a career conversation that is held during each position, or once every three years. This conversation encompassed personal developments and wishes for the near future. This personal development of the employee was necessary to keep them valuable to the organization. In addition to internal mobility, the career counselor paid attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section consists of four military offices for the service groups, namely the operational service, marines, technical service, and logistics service, and an office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of the year, this section had 37 military and three civilian positions. Career guidance for civilian personnel had been in place for over a year. The evaluation of this new phenomenon is currently ongoing and will be completed in 2019.

sections.text: 4_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-5 24 Directorate Personnel and Operations This year, various groups experienced personnel shortages. This was particularly evident among the junior officers and the middle management of the non-commissioned officers. Another concluded measure for personnel retention was that the constant shifting of personnel was minimized. An excessive number of first lieutenants of the Marines and corporals of the Technical Department was maintained to ultimately fill the scarcity in higher ranks. Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve The deployment of reservists has increased due to the introduction of the Adaptive Armed Forces. This led to a desired growth of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve and further professionalization. In 2018, the number of reservists grew by more than two hundred individuals. These were not only former colleagues but also people without prior military experience. This also meant that the hours of deployment increased compared to 2017. These reservists were appointed due to their accumulated experience in the civilian world and their specific expertise. A portion of this new intake joined the Navy through the Defensity College program. In this program, students are given the opportunity to work for one or two days a week during their bachelor’s and master’s studies for the Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën undergoing maintenance at the DMI in Den Helder.

sections.title: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.6)
sections.text: 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Management They are appointed as aspirant officers in the reserves. During their studies, they are trained as officers through military and additional training in leadership. After completing their studies, they choose to continue their career as reserve officers or to receive further training to become career officers. Bureau Flexible Capacity During the previous year, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established to gain more control over the deployment of flexible personnel. This referred to reservists, civilians, and temporarily available military personnel. In 2018, this bureau was further expanded with the introduction of a recruitment pool for civilian personnel. Bureau Flexible Capacity was a successful instrument that provided the organization with more insight into the need for flexible personnel and their expertise. Integration (INT) Head: Captain (ktz) A. van de Sande The Integration (INT) department is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations Management (DPBV), one of the three line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). Furthermore, small adjustments were made to the assessment system this year. A clearer distinction was made between formative and summative assessments. Watch Officer (VO)/IMO Since 2016, the VO specialization has been decoupled from the CCO training and transformed into the IMO training. This year, the training was also opened to watch officers with a Sea Watch Standard-B. Additionally, a preparatory module was developed so that the theoretical entry signal of the watch officers could be compared with that of the CCO. This module lasted three weeks and was provided prior to the IMO training, combined with the Warfare Introduction for Officers of the Marines communication service. Defense Sailing School (DVS) The year started well with the opening of the ZMST on February 21. The range of training was expanded with the ZMST, resulting in an increased presence of students on the Harssens peninsula. In contrast, the closure of the Dependence for daily operations took place. This decision was necessary due to the condition of the building. The personnel were temporarily housed with the other DVS personnel in the 'Klooster' at the KIM. Additionally, steps were taken to ensure that the planned new construction would not face further delays. Fortunately, the closure had only a minimal impact on the training, allowing all courses to proceed. The seamanship training unit conducted three EVO ODND courses in 2018, including an upgraded and a retraining variant, as well as a VVO ODND, which completed their BOZ training at the ZMST for the first time. Furthermore, many rubber boat, Rigid Hulled Inflatable Boat (RHIB), and crane training sessions were conducted. The navigation training unit provided, in addition to the regular training, four Navigation Modules <500 tons, a ZWST-K training, and a NATO GBW training last year. Due to low enrollment, the NATO Small Surface Units (KBW) course was canceled in 2018. The execution of the NATO GBW training was not without its challenges. After the required ships for practical sailing were unavailable in the first week, it was decided to halt the training. The amphibious sailing training was conducted by the training unit of the SSTG on Texel. They provided five LCRM, five Fast Raiding Interception and Special Forces Craft (FRISC), three LC BASIC, two LC3, and one LC2 training courses.

sections.text: 4_KM_Annual_Report_2018_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-27 46 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Binational training and exercises The crews of the Belgian and Dutch mine countermeasure units go to EGUERMIN to follow functional training: Enlisted personnel and non-commissioned officers from the Operational Service and naval officers learn to use various systems to detect and clear naval mines; Personnel from the Technical Service receive instruction on, among other things, the Degaussing System, which reduces the magnetic signature of the ships; Divers receive training on deck work and the operation of naval mines; Personnel responsible for deploying the Remote Environmental Monitoring Unit System (REMUS) Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) are trained at EGUERMIN to become REMUS 100 AUV Operators; Team training takes place in the TTF (Team Training Facility). The Marine Training Center in Rotterdam (MOC) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) X.E. van den Berg, from July 1 Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P. Damen The past year was busy with personnel changes, promotions, service time gratifications, and colleagues leaving the service. For the Marine Training Center, it was a year with three command transfers and a variety of training programs. It was also the year in which the task was assigned to revise the initial training and increase the recruitment assignment. This led to the 'charcoal sketch', which transitioned to four intakes and a split between the Basic Military Training (EMV) and EVO. This plan was developed in 2018 and presented in the AR. During the 440th meeting of the AR, the actual assignment was given to implement this plan starting in 2019. This year, the various training departments accomplished a lot of work. A total of 164 marines were delivered, 166 students completed their VeVa, the career training department delivered 11 midshipmen and 77 corporals. Additionally, eight sergeants and corporals were offered the sergeant training, and three cadre members were given the Commander Raiding Section training. The sports training program trained 15 cadre members. Besides these training programs, various support activities were carried out. Furthermore, there were several nice events, such as the annual performance of the Marine Band and the pub quiz at the beginning of the year. The joint sports day was held after the summer break, and the year concluded with the Corps anniversary and the accompanying Boxing Gala.

Documents that were initiated this year will continue into the future, while the need to provide specific education already started in 2018. In addition to providing and supporting educational development, the first steps were also taken to give shape to the project Learning Environment of the Future from OKM. The MOC was the driving force behind this project, which aimed to embody the credo 'learn anytime and anywhere.' sections.text: The Operations Directorate is on standby for the NATO Response Force. The main exercise for this was Trident Juncture 2018 as part of the Autumn Archer 2018 deployment in the autumn of 2018. During this exercise, the MBS commanded an ATG in an asymmetric, joint, and combined environment. sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-5 56 Operations Directorate Marine Training Command (MTC) Commander: LtCol (ltkolmarns) J.P.O. de Jong Shooting Competition in Poznan After a relatively quiet period, the shooting teams of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) – two teams from the Royal Netherlands Marine Reserve (KMR) and the Marine shooting team – participated again in September in the international NATO shooting competition Snajper in Poznan, Poland. Each team consisted of four shooters. In addition to the Dutch teams, teams from the United Kingdom, Czech Republic, Switzerland, Italy, France, Germany, and of course Poland also took part in the competition. A considerable international gathering with, as it turned out, many top shooters. This time, the competition took place at the outdoor range Biedrusko Military Training Ground near Poznan. The competition consists of seven events, where shooting is done with weapons supplied by and from the Polish army. Before a team begins shooting with a weapon, the procedures with the weapon are first practiced under the guidance of a Polish instructor. The instructor also assists the shooters at the shooting point. Although the Marine team achieved good results, they just missed out on the prizes. Fortunately, the KMR teams managed to win three awards; the second prize overall foreign team, the second prize overall individual, and the first prize for rifle. Sea Training Command (STC) Commander: Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar Last year, Commander Sea Training Command (C-STC) Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar was relieved on June 15 by Captain (ktz) R.W.J. Schoonen. It was a challenging annual program with a wide range of units to be trained. Some of these ships underwent the regular Safety And Readiness Check (SARC) process. Others were subjected to a CT or Pre Deployment Training (PDT). From January 15 to February 2, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt kicked off with a SARC-4 training near Great Britain. The first two weeks focused on maritime operations and the last week on amphibious operations. After completion, the ship was declared 'exercise ready' and could later in the year continue the process with Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST). At the end of February, the SARC-4 program, interrupted by Hurricane Irma, could finally resume.

The first part of the Blue Waves journey began on 1 April 2018, with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman serving as the flagship of Operation Sea Guardian. The ship conducted various operations in the Mediterranean Sea, focusing on maritime security and cooperation with allied forces.

During the second part of the Blue Waves journey, the Special Operations Forces Exercise (SOFEX) took place from 15 to 20 April 2018. This exercise involved complex scenarios that tested the capabilities of both the Dutch and Danish maritime Special Operations Forces. The cooperation between the two nations was highly successful, enhancing interoperability and joint operational effectiveness.

In May, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman returned to the Netherlands for maintenance and crew rest. The ship underwent necessary repairs and preparations for upcoming missions. The crew participated in various training exercises to maintain their readiness and operational skills.

In June, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was deployed again, this time for a multinational exercise in the North Sea. The exercise involved multiple NATO allies and focused on anti-submarine warfare and air defense operations. The ship demonstrated its capabilities in a challenging environment, working closely with allied forces to ensure maritime security.

Throughout the year, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman played a crucial role in various operations and exercises, showcasing the professionalism and dedication of its crew. The ship's successful deployments contributed significantly to the Royal Netherlands Navy's operational readiness and international cooperation efforts.

Integrating these units on Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was a challenge, as it had to be completed within one month. In addition to the integration, the JSS had to be assigned and all personnel and materials embarked. The crew also conducted a Force Protection Exercise in Den Helder, performed maintenance, and carried out normal operations. At the beginning of April, the ship set sail together with Zr.Ms. Holland. Both ships simultaneously conducted a PDT, during which the units trained together. The PDT and the final integration between units of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman were completed in one and a half weeks and concluded with a boarding on the Italian Navy ship ITS Orione. After this, the JSS was ready for the mission Operation Sea Guardian. Following a port visit to Cagliari in Sardinia, an exercise with Tunisian units was to take place near Bizerte. Unfortunately, this did not occur. The ship continued on its own course and began with imagery collection and investigated various Vessels of Combined Interest (VOCI). After one and a half weeks of sailing, the ship visited Aksaz (Turkey) for briefings from HQ-MARCOM with the Task Group of which Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was the flagship. The JSS formed a Task Group with TCG Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman as seen from a helicopter during Operation Sea Guardian in the Mediterranean Sea.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.11)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-11 62 Operations Directorate Gokceada and ITS Espero. After the port visit to Aksaz, the Task Group conducted a short period of CET/Force Integration Training (FIT), which concluded with a boarding by a team from ITS Espero on Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman and a multi Replenishment at Sea (RAS) with both ships. The conclusion of CET/FIT marked the start of the mission Operation Sea Guardian. This involved building a presence in the Mediterranean in areas designated by NATO. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman conducted presence operations near the coast of Libya. Two and a half weeks later, the mission was completed, and the ship sailed to Souda Bay, Greece, where the Role 2 Team and the Cougar detachment disembarked. The next part of the journey involved SOFEX. This was to conclude with a port visit to Tunis, but this could not take place. A new port was then found; the ship sailed via the Strait of Messina and the Strait of Bonifacio to Toulon. Here, the Dutch and Danish SOF (including two drones) units disembarked. Upon departure from Toulon, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman exercised with a French Landing Craft Utility (LCU) to take vehicles on board and return them to the LCU at the beach. During the transit to Lisbon, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman trained alongside FS Tonnere, with the ships conducting RAS approaches to each other. Ultimately, the exercise concluded with a real RAS. On the return journey from Lisbon, the ship received a second Cougar helicopter for the HQ week. During this, the units conducted both single spot and dual spot operations, after which the ship arrived in Den Helder in early June. June was focused on clearing the ship after the previous voyage. In the last week of June, the ship operated as a sparring partner for Zr.Ms. Friesland and BNS Leopold. In July, a sports day was organized for the entire crew by the OS&O committee. This was a successful day at the Haukes. Furthermore, a family sailing day took place this month. The following week was the CZSK relationship day, during which many units simultaneously conducted demonstrations. On this day, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman acted as Officer Conducting Exercise. The following units participated in the CZSK relationship day: BNS Leopold, BNS Crocus, Zr.Ms. Evertsen, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, Zr.Ms. Snellius, Zr.Ms. Walrus, SATG, two F-16s, NLMARSOF, the coast guard with a Dornier, 860 Squadron with an NH90, and the Joke Dijkstra from KNRM. During this day, another RAS was conducted with Zr.Ms. Evertsen. In September, the ship participated in a Non-Combatant Evacuation (NEO) operation together with the German Sea Battalion near Rostock. The exercise Schneller Adler was a large German exercise in which the Sea Battalion used Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman to evacuate personnel.

The Landing Platform Dock (LPD) served as her training trajectory for this purpose. During this period, the ship also functioned as a Helicopter Qualification (HQ) platform to certify deck flight crews and helicopter personnel. On April 9, the ship left Den Helder while the air force exercise Frisian Flag was simultaneously occurring. Once the last fighter jet had passed, the ship set course for Scotland to participate in the international exercise Joint Warrior under the command of Commodore Hulsker until May 10. After a period of scheduled maintenance in Den Helder, the LCF operated as an HQ platform in the North Sea from July 9 to July 13 to certify flight deck crews and helicopter personnel. Shortly thereafter, the crew went on summer leave from July 16 to August 17. After the personnel returned, the ship began its port work-up program on August 20 in preparation for deployment in SNMG2. During this timeframe, procedural training for warfare serials took place, the boarding team was trained under the guidance of the Force Protection & Boarding Operations (FPBO) section, and extensive Battle Damage Repair training was conducted in the Nieuwe Haven. sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.14)
sections.text: From September 5 to 9, Zr.Ms. Evertsen made its appearance during the World Port Days in Rotterdam. Many interested visitors toured the ship, which was moored in a prominent location at the quay. Immediately following the World Port Days, the ship departed for the Combat Training (CT), during which the vessel and its crew were tested to the limit in both the North Sea and the Danish training areas near the Kattegat. After returning to Den Helder on September 21, the port work program was resumed. This again focused on training the crew in all aspects of operating a naval ship. Therefore, the ship was in Den Helder until October 19. From October 22 to November 8, it was time for Zr.Ms. Evertsen to put all the learned skills into practice during the CT under the leadership of the Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST) in Plymouth. In preparation for the deployment in Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 (SNMG2), which started in January 2019, several information sessions were held after FOST, including for the families at home. The frigate was deployed from November 26 to 30 for NATO sailing exercises. After a few more personal training sessions for some crew members and the final preparations for the scheduled departure on January 5, 2019, the gangway was secured on December 17, and the crew could enjoy their Christmas leave. Launch of an SM-2 missile from Zr.Ms. Evertsen.

Sinke Zr.Ms. Groningen was primarily focused on BO and training for most of the year. At the beginning of January, the crew provided several weeks of personnel support to the Royal Marechaussee in executing Maritime Border Control in Europoort. In mid-February, the ship emerged from dry dock. After a successful SARC-1 in early June, the vessel was towed from the naval yard to the operational berths on June 19. Starting in September, the training period for the ship and crew began. This started with the schooling period in which crew members attended various service-related refresher courses. On September 20, one of the life rafts was tested. The crew was very enthusiastic, and marine vlogger Annelotte Zwart was present to document the test. From October 22 to 30, the crew was able to demonstrate what they had learned during the SARC-3 under the guidance of the STC. Due to issues with the main propulsion diesel, this did not go smoothly. Nevertheless, Zr.Ms. Groningen managed to complete the SARC-3 within five days. Following the SARC-3, there was a four-week period of Varende Materieels Beproevingen (VMB). This went well. During these weeks, the VLICO Zee was also successfully concluded. The weekend between the third and fourth week, the ship was in the port of Antwerp. This was the first port visit for the crew in this composition. It was unexpected that Zr.Ms. Groningen received the assignment to assist with NATO sailing practice. This meant an additional week of sailing after the VMBs. It became a busy week with many navigation exercises, while part of the crew remained behind to attend various training courses. On December 18, the traditional Christmas tree ceremony took place. A Christmas tree was previously hoisted in the mast to indicate that the ship was in port during the holidays so that other ships could send mail home. Bijleveld From November 18, 2018, to April 26, 2019, Zr.Ms. Zeeland was deployed as SSCG. Zr.Ms. Zeeland arrived in Curaçao in early December with a ceremonial entry. After a short logistical stop, Zr.Ms. Zeeland began executing its tasks. On the first patrol day, this immediately resulted in the interception of a transport with people without passports, who were handed over to the coast guard. In December, the ship facilitated the theme day of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean (CZMCARIB). This theme day focused on the (simplified) military assistance requests and strengthening cooperation with local authorities in Curaçao. One of the three main tasks of Defense in the Caribbean is to support local and civil authorities. At the initiative of CZMCARIB, discussions were held on board regarding how and in what situations military assistance can be of added value. Additionally, the procedure for requesting certain assistance in Curaçao was simplified. This allowed for quicker action. The simplified assistance procedure applied to the deployment of military search, military tracking, diving operations, and static observations with binoculars and drones. With an attendance of nearly seventy partners from the security chain, including (representatives of) the government, Curaçao Police Corps (KPC), the public prosecutor's office (OM), Justice, Coast Guard, Royal Marechaussee, the Governor's cabinet, Customs, and representation from the Netherlands, the theme day was a success. As a result, a similar day will be organized next year for the chain partners in Aruba. During the port visit to Kralendijk in Bonaire, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, in the context of the 'Open Day of Defense', held an open ship together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan. Here, the Army Company in the West (CidW), the Curaçao Militia (CURMIL), and the coast guard conducted various activities on the quay. Towards the end of the year, Zr.Ms. Zeeland intercepted a fast boat near Bonaire that was transporting a large illegal amount of cash. The naval ship also managed to disrupt a drug transport near the Windward Islands; during the interception action, the crew of a go-fast threw the contraband overboard to destroy evidence.

sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.38)
sections.text: Directorate Operations focuses on personnel management, faster procurement, implementing an industrial strategy, and developing cyber, Information Driven Operations (IGO), and disruptive technologies. Parallel to this publication, the Integrated Foreign and Security Policy was released, which also set new priorities. The development direction of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) had to primarily focus on innovation and concept development based on this. The role of the Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC) was evident in this. In June, Captain (ktz) H. Welmer took command of the MWC from Captain (ktz) K. Vooijs to fulfill the aforementioned objectives. After a process of intensive development and in collaboration with TNO, the MWC was able to declare the new Maritime Battlelab (MBL) Initial Operations Capable (IOC) in April 2018. The battlelab is an innovative concept to conduct high-end virtual simulations of (maritime) warfare scenarios. Applications for which the MBL was designed include concept development, pre-testing of launch scenarios, and post-simulation of executed launches. This can be done stand-alone, but also connected to a network of similar capabilities, primarily for concept development. Now the MWC has that capacity structurally in-house and could work on possibilities to generate the same capacity for underwater warfare. The possibilities that this capacity offered were endless, and given the attention that the MBL attracted, it was expected that more and more partners would work with this capacity and that more applications would be discovered. sections.title: Directie Operaties (p.39)
sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-39 90 Operations Directorate In February, the amphibious operations section was finally ready to publish its Maritime Doctrine Publication on Amphibious Operations. In March, the AR decided to continue the study on the Future Littoral Operating Concept (FLITOC). This process quickly became known as the 'roadmap mastering the littoral' (MTL). This was intended to lead to a complete revision of how operations from the sea are shaped. Given the small size of the MWC amphibious section, these activities are coordinated between MWC, S&A, and the group leader of the Marines. The roadmap describes a three-phase approach: from concept development, through force design to force development. This development is strongly coordinated with the United Kingdom and the United States, as they had recognized a similar need. This process is expected to take at least five years. After lengthy discussions, it was confirmed this year what had already been established in 2015 in a directive written by DGO. JKCMOX became the standard setter for Working at Height Cluster: “Operational climbing, descending, and moving on conditioned objects and in unconditioned environments using access, positioning, and fall protection techniques.” This meant that they determined what is safe and what is not for all climbing and descending techniques in an operational military context. This brought a whole stack of work with it, which meant that MWC was not in a hurry to carry out these activities on the bridge of Zr.Ms. Snellius.

Last year, the MWC also produced a series of publications. In Maritime Ballistic Missile Defence and Submarine Warfare, new concepts for future operations were established. Knowledge was documented for the CZSK-wide reader in the manuals Above Water Warfare and Use of Tactical Data Links in CZSK. Lastly, knowledge was also documented for a specific target group in the Manuals Military Tracking and Avalanche Safety. Hydrographic Service Chief Hydrographer: Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck Offer Development Within IHO cooperation, new standards were developed for the unlocking of hydrographic data. This was based on S-100, the Universal Hydrographic Data Model. The transition to S-100 and the associated product specifications will commence in the coming years. It remains to be seen how the service will prepare for this and what the implications will be for processes, products, and services. The Hydrographic Service (HYD) decided to discontinue several products, including a paper chart of the Northern coastal area. A difficult decision was the termination of the innovative product Digipilot, which had been on the market for about ten years. As a legacy from the paper era, the Electronic Naval Charts (ENC) had long followed the layouts and naming conventions of the paper charts. However, the connection between paper and electronic charts is fading. Additionally, the organization of ENCs had become confusing due to changes in paper chart numbers and the combined use of 1800 charts and nautical charts. Therefore, a new, grid-oriented organization of the ENC portfolio will be implemented gradually. Demand Development The trend from paper to digital continued in 2018. The expectation is that next year the trend will level off due to the requirement to carry ENCs for SOLAS ships >500GT by July 2018.

sections.text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-41 92 Operations Directorate The ratio between our own products and products under license has further decreased over the past year. Two important improvements have been made, which were agreed upon during the agents' meeting on October 22: The delivery of non-updated nautical charts is now described; The arrangement for returning expired copies has been expanded. The distribution of co-production charts with the United Kingdom Hydrographic Office (UKHO) was improved by connecting to their Print on Demand (PoD) system. HYD and UKHO made agreements about this in 2018 that will now be implemented. The formalization of those agreements will take place as part of the renewal of the Bilateral Arrangement with UKHO. The reuse of HYD's open data was further promoted through joining the collaboration Information House Marine (IHM). The partners wanted to further develop the IHM portal into a central place for maritime environmental information of the Dutch part of the North Sea, including the open data from HYD. The web services through which geographical names and the Dutch maritime boundaries and zones are offered as open data have been harmonized since May 3 according to the INSPIRE directive (Annex I). The implementation took a year and concluded with a visit from the auditors of the European Defence Agency (EDA) to the locations of the individual participants to conduct an audit. They also visited the Nieuwe Haven as the first defence location in the Netherlands with an energy management system. This pilot was led by Mr. R.J.L. Put from the EDB. General Unlike the previous year, there was a significant turnover in leadership positions within CZMCARIB. This also meant that the vision of the 2018 annual plan remained unchanged: “CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.” To make this vision realistic, a strategy was chosen where one team CARIB, maintaining the foundation, and strengthening partnerships in the region were the objectives. In 2017, CZMCARIB initiated various changes and projects in its operations, but these were not yet completed. In 2018, projects such as working with SAP, the introduction of new equipment, and the implementation of Assortimentsgewijs Werken in the Caribbean continued.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.4)
sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Station Ships C-ZMCARIB deployed four ships as SSCG under command in 2018. Throughout the year, Zr.Ms. Van Speijk, Zr.Ms. Holland, Zr.Ms. Friesland, and Zr.Ms. Zeeland carried out various tasks of the SSCG. All units are equipped with an NH90 onboard helicopter. This served as a force multiplier in various operations. Counter Drugs All station ships patrolled for both KW CARIB and Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG). Various successes were achieved. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 removed approximately 3000 kilograms of drugs from the illegal trade market in 2018. These international operations were undertaken with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, the United Kingdom, and the Dominican Republic. Hurricane Relief In preparation for the hurricane season, which ran from June 1 to November 30, CZMCARIB, together with local authorities, conducted the annual Hurricane Exercise (HUREX). These HUREX exercises were carried out at the unit level in Aruba and Curaçao and CZMCARIB-wide in the Windward Islands. Hurricane Relief Exercise On September 7, 2018, Hurricane Isaac developed over the Atlantic Ocean. Given the forecasts, it was possible that Isaac would pass through the Caribbean Sea as a hurricane, potentially causing damage to Dominica or the Windward Islands of the Kingdom. In preparation for this, CZMCARIB provided assistance to International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in maintaining international law and order in the Caribbean. Due to the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The Navy is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is also the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

Also in Curaçao, engineers from the CidW provided support to the KPC in searching the prison, residences, and properties as part of judicial investigations. Support was also provided from the Netherlands in the form of the Maritime Advance Search Team (MAST) of the Korps Mariniers. SARGASSUM. The CidW and CURMIL provided assistance in Bonaire and Curaçao by clearing large amounts of washed-up sargassum. Carnival and Harvest Festival. On Sint Maarten, the Marine Detachment on the island assisted in securing the penitentiary institution. In Bonaire, the CidW supported the relocation of the penitentiary institution. The 32 RSQN and the CidW provided assistance several times through static observations. In Curaçao, assistance was provided multiple times to safety partners with diving capacity. Soft military assistance was also provided by storing vehicles at barracks that had been confiscated by so-called seizure teams.

Engineers from CidW executed various projects, including the construction of a jump bunker and a hand grenade range at the Wacawa training area and various activities at Marine Base Parera (MBPAR), Marine Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF), and MS-KSAV. Additionally, the CidW supported various charities in both Curaçao and Bonaire. The rotations frequently assisted the local authorities in Curaçao with search operations using their engineering capabilities. Each rotation conducted integrated training and exercises with the Beteugelen van Woelingen Platoon (BVW Platoon) alongside the KPC and the Volunteer Corps Curaçao. These trainings were consistently led by the Integrated Professional Skills Training (IBT) instructors from the Royal Marechaussee. Engineers from the 41st Armored Engineer Battalion practiced with heavy explosives in Curaçao.

Finances In 2018, there was a break in trend regarding expenditures and the allocated budget. Instead of "putting the brakes on" expenditures, these were stimulated in 2018. This led to the initially allocated budget for CZMCARIB being increased throughout the year. As a result, it became possible to realize infrastructural projects to improve living and working conditions ahead of schedule. With the introduction of the "independent small purchases" procedure, goods and services could be acquired more quickly and easily without the intervention of the procurement office. The limited purchasing capacity of CZMCARIB could thus be utilized for important and financially significant dossiers. Velas Latin America Curaçao From Sunday, July 17 to Wednesday, July 19, the port of Curaçao hosted nine tall ships. The reason for their visit was the maritime event VLAC. In the spring of 2018, MBPAR facilitated the organization of this maritime event. The local Sail Foundation Curaçao had overall leadership but relied heavily on CZMCARIB. A large part of the requested support was also provided by MBPAR, including a project leader. In the preparation and execution, the naval base maintained liaison with the VLAC organization and directed the project team of CZMCARIB. It was a successful event, during which an informal request came from the Curaçao Sail Foundation to CZMCARIB to participate again in 2022 or to provide support. 

Personnel - Accommodation Last year, the accommodation at MBPAR had 205 beds, spread over 114 rooms. The accommodation met the standards of the time and was, as already indicated, used intensively. Although there was ample capacity for sleeping places, the demand for accommodation increased throughout the year. As a result, external hotel accommodation was regularly called upon. Emergency sleeping accommodation in the sports hall of the naval base was also utilized.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.15)

The barracks Landkrab and Zeeschildpad were painted during the past period, as well as the Goudenbal. All rooms are equipped with a faster wifi connection, and construction is underway for a new bar in the Longroom. The Personnel - Physical Training & Sports and Development & Recreation (FT&S/O&O) Bureau O&O reflected on a successful 2018 filled with enjoyable events for young and old. Additionally, cross-pollination between the various departments is important for the continued development of the services that this office can provide. Naval Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF) Commander: Major (majmarns) C. van Dinteren The barracks has become the Caribbean Training Center (OCC), as part of OKM. sections.text: 7_KM_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-17 134 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean conducted training simultaneously: the EMV, the VVO, and the Practical Training for Officer Caribbean (POTOC). After an intensive recruitment and selection period, 30 out of 68 registered candidates started the EMV training in 2018. This year, eighteen militia members from Aruba and Curaçao began the VVO. By the end of 2018, the training was well over halfway completed. After a Pre-POTOC phase, two CURMIL candidates traveled to the Netherlands in October to complete phases 1 and 2 of the Practical Training for Officer of the Marines (POTOM). Military ceremony during the annual Opening of the States on September 10.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.18)
sections.text: 7_KM_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-18 135 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean The Social Training Program (SVT) could not take place in 2018 due to the restructuring by the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sport not being completed. The SVT is a training program of approximately five months. This program is aimed at bringing about a positive behavioral change in disadvantaged youth who, for various reasons, have found themselves on the margins of society. The ambition for an SVT implementation in 2019 is high on the agenda. In 2018, the Training Center provided various functional training courses and programs. A core instructor training for Patrol Search took place, with twelve trainees from CARMIL and one trainee from the Volunteer Corps Curaçao (VKC) passing. The retraining of the CURMIL Green Platoon in search operations was facilitated. Additionally, a pilot search training was conducted by the OCC in the field of Search for the KPA. In conclusion, ten driving courses for military C driver's licenses were provided, and dozens of retrainings for IVECO and the Mercedes-Benz 280CDI were carried out. The green and blue platoon CURMIL The CURMIL green platoon is the operationally deployable unit. The Ministry of Justice requested CZMCARIB for assistance in the form of hard and soft military support. Operation Ta Basta Awor (TBA), loosely translated as "Now is Enough," is one example of CURMIL's deployment of hard military assistance. In TBA, the focus is on reducing illegal possession of firearms. The operation was carried out throughout the year 2018, in good consultation and always together with the KPC, frequently. In this context, CURMIL's tasks were expanded with vehicle search authorities. An example of soft military assistance is the integrated operation during Carnival 2018, where CURMIL and KPC acted as partners to ensure public safety. With various national and international training sessions, CURMIL continuously worked on readiness. The added value of CURMIL as a partner for the visiting units became increasingly well-known, and requests for assistance grew. Last year, much time was invested in further intensifying the social relevance of CURMIL in Curaçao. Examples of this included charity actions such as work on the children's care pavilion at the Christian foundation Siloam; organizing and executing various sports activities for elementary school children; conducting recruitment programs at secondary schools; supporting national holidays; and carrying out many ceremonial tasks.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.19)
sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-19 136 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Security, Environment, and Health As a barracks in general and as a training center in particular, (physical and social) safety was a high priority on the MKSUF agenda in 2018. Through fixed contracts, the barracks and its individual spaces were kept clean, safe, and free of pests. The intrinsic perception of the MKSUF personnel regarding these issues was high in 2018, as evidenced by the results of inspections and audits conducted by (external) defense and government services; all were passed with a (well) sufficient rating. For primary healthcare, the MKSUF personnel utilized the Primary Healthcare (EGB) health center at MBPAR. Military ceremony during the annual Opening of the States in Curaçao.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.22)
sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean 32nd Marine Squadron In line with the ambition to strengthen partnerships, the 32nd Marine Squadron (32 RSQN) invested in collaboration with local partner services in 2018. To ultimately become the relevant security partner in the region in general and Aruba in particular, further engagement was sought with the local disaster management staff; police, fire brigade, and coast guard. This collaboration led to various forms of deployment in 2018. With the simplified application procedure, several capabilities of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZM-CARIB) were quickly deployable for the Caribbean islands within the Kingdom. As a result, the 32 RSQN was deployed several times for searching objects, tracking, and observing. Ultimately, the unit was deployed three times for static observation in support of the Public Prosecution Service and the coast guard. Additionally, it provided support three times for search operations in Curaçao and once in Aruba in support of the Public Prosecution Service. In 2018, the marines supported the coast guard in large-scale operations and specific assignments. Marines also assisted on the coast guard cutters in carrying out coast guard tasks. In 2018, the unit began providing a Guard Team for the station ship. This team can conduct boardings on vessels as part of anti-drug operations. The 32 RSQN was also on standby to carry out any emergency assistance operations, including humanitarian aid. As Tropical Storm Isaac approached, the units were moved to the Windward Islands in preparation for assistance after a possible destructive passage. A troop was moved to Curaçao and embarked on the station ship Caribbean Area, and a troop including squadron staff was flown in advance to Sint Maarten. The unit on this last island provided support to the local police. Due to the weakening of the storm, the unit on board the station ship was ultimately not deployed. In Aruba, the 32 RSQN provided support for the readiness of various safety services. The unit supported or organized various disaster exercises. For example, the unit participated in March in the exercise Carib Wave with different scenarios, ranging from a tsunami that had caused damage to the island to a tabletop exercise involving a bomb threat on board a cruise ship. For the runway overshoot exercise, the unit provided simulated casualties, simulating an aircraft accident. The unit also organized a hurricane exercise on the island, sharing experiences from Hurricane Irma in 2017.

sections.title: Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.24)
sections.text: Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied The unit received and supported several units in Aruba during training and education. Together with the barracks, it provided support in 2018 for: A diving training from the United States Marine Corps; The military tracker (instructor) course; The Basic and Advanced training of the local militias; The training for frogmen; The training of the CidW of Curaçao; Ceremonial tasks during Dia di Bandera, Dia di Betico, King's Day, Remembrance Day, and the three arrivals of the station ship in Aruba; The events Highwinds (surf and wakeboard event) and the Aruba Regatta (sailing). In addition to deployment and support, the unit conducted various training sessions in 2018 to maintain or improve training and operational readiness. With the exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior at Camp Lejeune in the United States, the unit carried out its annual exchange with the American Marines in March. In this exercise, the unit was trained in operations in urban areas. The unique training location and opportunities at Camp Lejeune provide added value to the training level of the unit. In June, the unit underwent its annual preparations for the hurricane season. With the exercise in Aruba, the entire unit was deployed. Subsequently, the staff of the unit traveled to Sint Maarten for the hurricane exercise in the Windward Islands. Here, further agreements were made with the island authorities regarding support and military assistance in the event of a possible hurricane passage, together with the Marine detachment Sint Maarten. Due to the support during tropical storm Isaac, the annual tactical and dynamic shooting exercise in Curaçao could not be carried out. This was then adjusted and executed in Aruba. The tactical exercise was subsequently expanded in preparation for the exercise Tres Kolos. The emphasis was on cooperation with the French unit from Martinique. The two-week exercise was divided into a team competition and a tactical final exercise. After winning the team competition, the squadron began the tactical final scenario, in which the French and Dutch units had to carry out a simultaneous attack.

sections.text: Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Logistics and Equipment Head: Lieutenant Commander (ltz1) M.C. Philipse-Breitenstein Due to the procurement office being understaffed throughout the year, needs could not always be met in a timely manner. By the end of the year, the department was fully staffed, allowing for a catch-up. A contract was signed for universal and Toyota parts for the white vehicle fleet. The mechanics and carpenter received large water-cooled fans, modeled after those in Curaçao, to improve working conditions. The IVECO was successfully introduced, and at the beginning of next year, the Anaconda will replace the MB280. The Supply Office received an environmental container to responsibly store chemical waste until it can be disposed of. The lighting in the warehouse is now compliant with Occupational Health and Safety (ARBO) requirements and energy-saving, and the fans in the warehouses have been repaired by the Rijks Vastgoedbedrijf (RVB). Sustainability This year, further steps were taken in the area of energy savings. In 2018, there was a 15% reduction in electrical energy consumption compared to the previous year. This was achieved by replacing air conditioning remote controls in combination with the use of timers between the air conditioners. Next year, savings could be expanded to 25 to 30% through further rollout. After that, we will depend on the RVB to meet the need for energy neutrality or even energy independence. To achieve this, approximately 4000 solar panels of 1.2MWp need to be added alongside the current panels of 100kWp. Together with battery capacity and the reconfiguration of generators and transformers at the barracks, this could lead to energy independence. This plan has been approved by the Minister of Defence. Furthermore, the Minister of Energy of Aruba, Elmar, has requested the electricity company in Aruba to cooperate. sections.text: 7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-29 146 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Cooperation One of the highlights of 2018 was the military assistance during storm Isaac. Leading up to this, there was no military assistance provided, causing the 96-hour deadline for the hurricane to pass. In the subsequent Emergency Operational Centre (EOC) meeting, it was decided to request military assistance. CZMCARIB managed to deploy the requested units before the expected passage. The task for this assistance was also clear beforehand: to support the local authorities in maintaining public order and safety. For this purpose, the Sint Maarten Police Corps (KPSM) shared their operational plan with CZMCARIB, and this was executed jointly with KPSM. Fortunately, the impact of storm Isaac was limited. Also, in 2018, a HUREX was conducted on Sint Maarten where, at the operational level, marines from the 32 RSQN, the Marine Detachment Sint Maarten (DETSXM), and all safety partners went through a multidisciplinary scenario. Visibility In 2017, military deployment ceased after hurricane Irma, and the detachment operated an adjusted program until the end of that year. As a result, in 2018, with a regular training program, extra attention was still paid to visibility in the Windward Islands. Each rotating element (every four months) carried out a so-called charity week. During these weeks, several small community projects were undertaken. Additionally, the detachment was also active on Saba and Sint Eustatius. On Saba, at the beginning of 2018, the triathlon was supported with participants and volunteers, marking the start of a collaboration between the organization and DETSXM. Disaster exercises on Saba and Sint Eustatius were also supported. Observation As part of the annual plan, the support point contributed to improving the information position of CZMCARIB by closely observing and reporting on the security situation in the area. This was done by conducting observation exercises on the SSS islands. These exercises were carried out in good consultation with the local safety partner. The observation skills of the rotating element were one of the capabilities that the safety partners did not possess, but for which there was a great need.

sections.text: Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean has, over the past few years, made significant progress in addressing the backlog of national decisions (appointment decisions). In the autumn of 2017, HR Caribbean Personnel, in consultation with representatives from HRM Caribbean Personnel, ARUMIL, and the Departmento Recurso Humano of Aruba, developed a renewed flow policy for ARUMIL. This new policy has led to considerable improvements in the legal status of ARUMIL. A positive flow decision is now linked to the militia of ARUMIL when their initial employment contract is nearing its end. In practice, this positive flow decision was often associated with a decision to participate in the VVO (Voluntary Military Service). Upon completion of the VVO, militia members of ARUMIL were appointed as civil servants rather than as contract workers. This civil servant status provided a preferential position when the involved militia member transitioned to the Government of Aruba. By decision of March 6, this new policy was established by the Council of Ministers of Aruba. By decision of April 25, the Minister of Defense indicated that they would finance the accumulation of pensions and link it to the aforementioned positive flow decision. It was the responsibility of the OBL to implement the established control measures. This aimed to further embed CZMCARIB safety in the line, the so-called first line of defense. With this method of working, the tasks and responsibilities regarding safety were particularly assigned and aligned with the element of 'structure'. In 2018, a portion of all operational TRAs was completed. Due to issues with the availability of the renewed SharePoint environment, these TRAs could not yet be published. Various technical and organizational causes underlie this. The goal was to resolve this issue as quickly as possible in close consultation with the project holder in Den Helder. In addition to the combined training and exercises for operational readiness, the voyage also focused on the education and motivation of second-year cadets from the Naval Service Corps. After completing the basic theoretical naval training at the Royal Naval Institute (KIM), they were tasked with translating this into practical skills as naval officers on a naval ship. Last year, a group of 35 cadets participated in the deployment. After two weeks, a rotation took place to provide all aspiring naval officers with an equal practical experience. The emphasis was on safe navigation in busy shipping areas, accurate positioning, seamanship exercises, and participation in the large international exercise BALTOPS 18. The planned port visits provided the cadets with an opportunity to present themselves as good ambassadors of the Dutch Armed Forces during various courtesy visits. The sailing program of the six-week voyage took place in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and around the Danish islands. Installation of cadets.

The banner of the Corps of Cadets is the oldest banner of the Royal Netherlands Navy. In 1904, Queen Wilhelmina presented the banner to the Corps. This banner is unique in the Dutch armed forces as it is the only one that is not orange but red, as the cadets had a corps flag in those colors before 1904. During the May days of 1940, it was even brought to safety by some cadets and taken to Great Britain. Unfortunately, the banner cloth itself has been subject to wear and has been replaced over the years. Last year, the banner was also due for replacement. The applications on the cloth, the anchor, the royal crown, and the text have been embroidered using a 3D technique, giving it more relief. The worn cloth has been added to the collection of the naval museum.
